content: A lens is an optical device that exhibits axial symmetry and is designed to transmit and refract light. It can either converge or diverge a beam of light. A simple lens consists of a single optical element, while a compound lens is made up of multiple simple lenses aligned along a common axis. The use of multiple elements in a compound lens allows for the correction of more optical aberrations than a single lens element can achieve. Lenses are typically manufactured from glass or transparent plastic. Additionally, materials that refract electromagnetic radiation outside the visible spectrum, such as paraffin wax for microwave lenses, are also referred to as lenses. The term lense is an archaic spelling, and only Merriam-Webster's medical dictionary recognizes it as correct. The earliest known lens artifact, made of rock crystal, dates back to approximately 640 BC and was discovered in Nineveh. Written references to lenses appear in Ancient Greece, such as Aristophanes' play The Clouds (424 BC), which mentions a burning-glass—a biconvex lens used to focus sunlight to ignite fires. Roman writings, including those of Pliny the Elder, also describe burning-glasses and possibly the first use of a corrective lens, as Nero reportedly used an emerald to view gladiatorial games, likely to correct myopia. Both Pliny and Seneca the Younger noted the magnifying effect of a glass globe filled with water. The term lens originates from the Latin word for lentil, as the shape of a double-convex lens resembles a lentil seed. The Arabian mathematician Ibn Sahl (c. 940–c. 1000) applied what is now known as Snell's law to calculate lens shapes. Ibn al-Haytham (965–1038) wrote the Book of Optics, which described how the human eye's lens forms an image on the retina. In the 11th to 12th centuries, the Vikings produced high-quality rock crystal lenses, known as Visby lenses, with imaging capabilities comparable to mid-20th-century aspheric lenses. These lenses could concentrate sunlight to ignite fires. The widespread use of lenses began with reading stones in the 11th century and the invention of spectacles in Italy during the 1280s. Nicholas of Cusa first recognized the benefits of concave lenses for myopia correction in 1451. Ernst Abbe's sine condition, developed in the 1860s, revolutionized optical instrument design by enabling sharp imaging of both on-axis and off-axis objects, significantly advancing technologies like microscopes. Most lenses are spherical, meaning their surfaces are segments of spheres. These surfaces can be convex (bulging outward), concave (curving inward), or planar (flat). The axis of the lens is the line connecting the centers of the spheres forming the lens surfaces. Lenses may be modified after manufacturing to alter their shape or size, which can shift the lens axis away from the physical center. Toric or spherocylindrical lenses have surfaces with different curvatures in orthogonal planes, resulting in varying focal powers across different meridians. Aspheric lenses, which have surfaces that are not spherical or cylindrical, can reduce optical aberrations more effectively than standard lenses. Lenses are categorized based on the curvature of their optical surfaces. A biconvex lens has two convex surfaces, while a biconcave lens has two concave surfaces. A plano-convex lens has one flat and one convex surface, and a plano-concave lens has one flat and one concave surface. A convex-concave lens, or meniscus lens, has one convex and one concave surface. Meniscus lenses are commonly used in corrective eyewear. Positive or converging lenses, such as biconvex or plano-convex lenses, focus parallel light beams to a point behind the lens, known as the focal point. Negative or diverging lenses, such as biconcave or plano-concave lenses, spread parallel light beams, making them appear to originate from a point in front of the lens. Meniscus lenses can be either positive or negative, depending on the relative curvatures of their surfaces. The focal length of a lens, which determines its optical power, can be calculated using the lensmaker's equation. The sign of the radii of curvature for the lens surfaces indicates whether they are convex or concave. For thin lenses, the focal length is positive for converging lenses and negative for diverging lenses. The thin lens equation relates the object distance, image distance, and focal length, enabling the calculation of image formation. A positive lens can form real images, which can be projected onto a screen, or virtual images, which appear on the same side of the lens as the object. Virtual images, such as those created by magnifying glasses, cannot be projected but can be observed through the lens. Lenses are subject to various optical aberrations, which distort the image quality. Spherical aberration occurs because spherical lens surfaces are not ideal for focusing light, causing blurring. Aspheric lenses, which have non-spherical surfaces, can minimize spherical aberration. Coma is another aberration that affects off-axis points, creating comet-like flares in the image. Chromatic aberration arises from the dispersion of light, where different wavelengths are refracted to different focal points, resulting in color fringes. This can be reduced using achromatic doublets or apochromatic lenses, which combine materials with different dispersive properties. Other aberrations include field curvature, distortion (barrel and pincushion), and astigmatism. Even with minimized aberrations, image quality is ultimately limited by diffraction due to the finite aperture of the lens. Compound lenses, which combine multiple simple lenses, can correct for many aberrations. The combined focal length of thin lenses in contact is determined by the sum of their optical powers. When separated by a distance, the back focal length (BFL) of the system depends on the separation and the individual focal lengths. An afocal system, where the separation equals the sum of the focal lengths, transforms a collimated beam into another collimated beam, as seen in telescopes. The magnification of such systems depends on the focal lengths of the lenses used. Lenses have numerous applications, including magnifying glasses, corrective eyewear, and imaging systems like microscopes, cameras, and telescopes. Convex lenses can focus sunlight to a point, generating enough heat to ignite materials, a principle used in burning glasses. Modern applications include concentrating solar energy onto photovoltaic cells and refracting electromagnetic radiation in radio astronomy and radar systems.
